narrative: The model estimates a 37% chance that you will fail your final year, and that estimate is high enough to place you in the failing-risk group that must take remedial courses. This is not a certainty, but it means the model sees warning signs that need action. The strongest factor behind the concern is your record of one past class failure, while students who passed had an average of none; this was the main feature pushing the prediction toward failing. The next two most influential factors actually worked in your favor. You come from a small household of three or fewer, which was less common among passing students, and you want to pursue higher education, as all passing students did; both pushed the prediction toward passing, but they were not strong enough to outweigh the past-failure signal. To improve your chances, treat the remedial courses seriously and use them to close gaps from that earlier failure. Increase weekly study time, which is currently under two hours while most passing students studied two to five hours, and keep using your family’s educational support. Speak with your teachers about a realistic study plan and ask for school support if difficulties arise.
